title: MoA: Mixture of Sparse Attention for Automatic Large Language Model Compression

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to overcome the limitation of uniform sparse-attention masks, which ignore diverse attention patterns and accuracy-latency trade-offs across heads and input lengths. Paper [14] explicitly addresses this same problem, stating: "Existing methods typically employ a single window length across all attention heads and input sizes. However, this uniform approach fails to capture the heterogeneous attention patterns inherent in LLMs, ignoring their distinct accuracy-latency trade-offs." This is substantively equivalent to the stated purpose.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces "heterogeneous elastic rules," where each attention head gets its own local attention span that scales elastically with input length, instead of a single uniform span/scaling for all heads. Paper [14] proposes "Mixture of Attention Spans," which similarly assigns heterogeneous sliding-window lengths to attention heads to optimize accuracy-latency trade-offs. Both mechanisms involve assigning distinct, locally adaptive attention spans to heads, making them substantively equivalent.

### Evaluation
The contribution improves fact retrieval accuracy from 25% to 98% compared with masks using a uniform span and scaling function for each head. Paper [14] evaluates its method using accuracy improvements in LLM inference efficiency tasks, which is substantively equivalent in evaluation design. Both use accuracy as the metric and compare heterogeneous attention spans against uniform ones, making the evaluation covered.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of LLM inference efficiency and long-context sparse attention. Paper [14] explicitly works in the same domain, targeting "LLM inference efficiency with heterogeneous sliding-window lengths" for long-context scenarios. This is substantively equivalent in application area.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to "automatically find the optimal per-head sparse-attention compression plan under a density budget."  
- **Paper [11]** ("Mixture of Attention Spans") optimizes LLM inference efficiency by selecting heterogeneous sliding-window lengths per attention head, which aligns with the goal of optimizing sparse attention configurations per head under constraints.  
- **Paper [7]** ("Online Weight Pruning Via Adaptive Sparsity Loss") addresses automatic pruning under a user-defined budget constraint, which is conceptually similar to optimizing sparse configurations under a density budget.  
Both papers share the same problem-class objective of optimizing resource allocation under constraints, albeit in different contexts.

### Mechanism
The contribution's mechanism is "an automatic optimization pipeline using gradient-based profiling of each attention position's influence on prediction loss, cast as a Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) problem to select elastic rules per head."  
- **Paper [4]** ("A Dynamic Resource Allocation Model for A Machine Requirements Problem") uses MIP for resource allocation optimization, which matches the underlying primitive of casting optimization problems as MIP.  
- **Paper [9]** ("Mixed Integer Polynomial Programming") reformulates optimization problems using MIP, demonstrating equivalence in the use of MIP for solving constrained optimization problems.  
- **Paper [17]** ("Identifying Critical Neurons in ANN Architectures using Mixed Integer Programming") applies MIP to neural network pruning, which is analogous to using MIP for selecting sparse attention rules per head.  
These papers demonstrate substantive equivalence in the mechanism of using MIP for optimization tasks.

### Evaluation
The contribution's evaluation design involves metrics like effective context length, retrieval accuracy, throughput comparisons, and relative performance drop reduction across multiple LLMs.  
- **Paper [11]** ("Mixture of Attention Spans") evaluates sparse attention methods using throughput, accuracy, and latency metrics across LLMs, which matches the evaluation design of comparing performance metrics across models.  
- **Paper [22]** ("SALO") evaluates hybrid sparse attention mechanisms using similar metrics like throughput and memory efficiency, aligning with the contribution's evaluation design.  
Both papers reuse the same evaluation design of benchmarking sparse attention methods across LLMs using standard performance metrics.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of "LLM inference efficiency / long-context sparse attention."  
- **Paper [1]** ("SampleAttention") addresses sparse attention for long-context LLM inference, which is the same application area.  
- **Paper [3]** ("Quest") focuses on efficient long-context LLM inference using query-aware sparsity, which also falls within the same domain.  
- **Paper [11]** ("Mixture of Attention Spans") optimizes sparse attention for LLM inference efficiency, directly overlapping with the contribution's domain.  
These papers confirm that the domain is covered.

**PURPOSE: Automatically find the optimal per-head sparse-attention compression plan under a density budget.**

Paper [11] is the most directly relevant — it is literally titled "Mixture of Attention Spans: Optimizing LLM Inference Efficiency with Heterogeneous Sliding-Window Lengths" and explicitly states it addresses "a single window length across all attention heads" by proposing MoA "which automatically..." assigns heterogeneous attention spans per head under efficiency constraints. This is substantively equivalent: same objective (find optimal per-head sparse attention plan under a budget), same target quantity (per-head compression allocation).

Paper [1] (SampleAttention) also pursues "dynamically capturing head-specific sparse patterns" for near-lossless acceleration, which is related but focuses on runtime dynamic selection rather than offline optimization of a plan.

Paper [11] clearly covers the purpose.

---

**MECHANISM: Gradient-based profiling of each attention position's influence on prediction loss, cast as a Mixed-Integer Programming problem to select elastic rules per head.**

This mechanism has two components: (a) gradient-based importance scoring of attention positions, and (b) MIP formulation to select per-head rules under a budget.

For (a): Papers [26], [29], [18] use gradient/Taylor-expansion-based importance estimation for pruning neural network components. Paper [26] explicitly "estimates the contribution of a neuron (filter) to the final loss" using Taylor expansions — this is the same primitive as gradient-based profiling of each position's influence on prediction loss.

For (b): Paper [17] introduces "a mixed integer program (MIP) for assigning importance scores to each neuron in deep neural network architectures which is guided by the impact of their simultaneous pruning on the main learning task." This is substantively equivalent — MIP formulation for selecting which components to prune/keep under a budget, guided by loss impact.

The combination of gradient-based profiling + MIP for per-head selection: Paper [17] covers the MIP-for-neural-component-selection primitive, and [26] covers gradient-based importance. However, no single paper combines both into a pipeline for per-head attention span selection. Paper [11] proposes MoA but its mechanism for finding the optimal plan is what this contribution claims to improve/automate — the question is whether [11] already uses this mechanism. The abstract of [11] says it "automatically" assigns spans, suggesting some optimization, but the specific gradient+MIP pipeline is the claimed novelty here.

Paper [17] covers the MIP-for-pruning-under-budget primitive. Paper [26] covers gradient-based loss-influence scoring. Together these cover both sub-primitives of the mechanism, even if no single paper combines them in this exact way. Since the question is whether any prior paper contains a substantively equivalent element per facet, [17] covers the MIP component and [26] covers the gradient profiling component. I'll cite [17] as the closest single-paper match for the MIP-based selection mechanism (which is the more distinctive part), noting [26] for gradient profiling.

---

**EVALUATION: ~2 hours optimization time; retrieval accuracy, throughput vs FlashAttention2/vLLM, max relative performance drop — on Vicuna-{7B,13B} and Llama3-{8B,70B}.**

The evaluation design uses: (1) needle-in-haystack / retrieval accuracy benchmarks for long-context LLMs, (2) throughput comparison against FlashAttention2 and vLLM baselines, (3) performance drop metrics. 

Paper [11] (MoA) evaluates on similar LLMs with similar metrics (accuracy-latency trade-offs for long-context). Paper [3] (Quest) evaluates long-context LLM inference efficiency with retrieval/accuracy metrics. Paper [1] (SampleAttention) evaluates TTFT and accuracy on long-context benchmarks.

The evaluation design (retrieval accuracy on long-context benchmarks + throughput vs. standard attention baselines) is used in [1], [3], and [11]. This is a standard evaluation design for long-context sparse attention papers.

---

**DOMAIN: LLM inference efficiency / long-context sparse attention.**

Papers [1], [3], [6], [8], [11], [22] all work in LLM inference efficiency with sparse/long-context attention. This domain is clearly covered.
